opus-5.5.text:
I think it holds up reasonably well, though I'd frame it a bit differently now than I did at the time. The appeal of agreement was that it's one of the cleanest cases where you can point to a dependency that's clearly sensitive to hierarchical structure rather than linear order. In a sentence like "the keys to the cabinet are on the table," the verb has to agree with "keys," not with "cabinet," even though "cabinet" is closer. So if a model gets that right, especially when there are intervening nouns with the opposite number, those "attractors," it's at least suggestive that it's tracking something like syntactic structure. And practically, it was a nice test case because you can generate lots of examples from naturally occurring text, and you don't need the model to do anything other than what it already does, which is predict the next word. You just compare the probability of "are" versus "is."

Looking back, a few things stand out. One is that it was useful partly because it was such a narrow, well-understood phenomenon. Linguists and psycholinguists had studied agreement attraction in humans for decades, so we had a baseline for what kinds of errors are "humanlike" and what kinds aren't. That made it possible to ask not just whether the network gets it right, but whether its errors pattern like people's errors, which I think is a more interesting question.

The other thing is that I'd be more cautious now about what success on agreement tells you. Getting agreement right on average in corpus sentences turned out to be easier than we initially thought, partly because a lot of the examples don't actually require structure; there are heuristics that get you most of the way. That's part of why we, and others, moved toward more controlled, constructed test sets, and why I became interested in the broader question of how you'd build evaluations that can distinguish genuine structural generalization from shallow cues.

So I think it was a good starting point. It was concrete and diagnostic, and it connected to a real body of human data. But it's one phenomenon, and the field rightly moved toward batteries of tests across many constructions, and toward asking how models generalize from the data they actually see.

r001.rationale: The response says agreement was easier for models than initially thought, but does not communicate that researchers were initially surprised LSTMs could handle it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it holds up reasonably well, honestly, though partly for reasons I didn't fully appreciate at the time. When Emmanuel Dupoux, Yoav Goldberg and I started that work around 2016, the question we were asking was pretty simple: these recurrent networks are getting very good at predicting the next word, but is that because they've picked up something like syntactic structure, or because they're exploiting shallow regularities in the sequence? Agreement was attractive because it's one of the cleanest cases where the two come apart. In a sentence like "the keys to the cabinet are on the table," the verb has to agree with "keys," not with "cabinet," which is the closer noun. If a model just tracks the most recent noun, it fails. If it has some notion of what the subject is, it succeeds. And crucially, you can test this at scale without any annotation beyond what you can extract automatically from the corpus, so it fit the style of work that was possible then.

Looking back, a few things stand out. One is that the result was more mixed than people sometimes remember. LSTMs trained purely as language models did pick up agreement in the easy cases, but they fell apart fairly quickly as you put more intervening material between subject and verb, and especially when there were attractors of the opposite number. That nuance got flattened somewhat in the retelling, both by people who wanted to say "neural networks learn syntax" and people who wanted to say they don't.

The second thing is that it turned out to be the beginning of a much larger program, what became targeted syntactic evaluation and then things like BLiMP and the whole family of minimal-pair benchmarks. I think the methodological contribution, the idea that you should construct controlled contrasts rather than just look at perplexity, ended up being more durable than any particular finding about LSTMs. Transformers made the specific model obsolete pretty fast, but the way of asking the question is still around.

If I'm being self-critical, I'd say we were maybe too quick to read behavioral success as evidence for a particular kind of representation. A model that gets agreement right could be doing it in lots of ways, and we didn't have great tools for distinguishing them. That's something the interpretability work since then has started to address. And I'd also say agreement, as a phenomenon, is a bit of a low bar. It's local in a certain sense, it's extremely frequent in the training data, and it's not obvious that getting it right tells you much about the harder compositional questions. So it was a good first test, but I'd be cautious about anyone who treats it as the test.

r001.rationale: The response describes agreement as a clean test and, in retrospect, a low bar that LSTMs handled in easy cases. It does not communicate that the researchers were initially surprised LSTMs could handle agreement, so the required contrast is incomplete.

astra-6.text:
I think it was a useful place to start because it gave us a very concrete question. A language model can be good at predicting words for lots of reasons, and we wanted to know whether it was learning something about syntactic structure. Subject-verb agreement lets you make that question quite precise: can the model identify the subject that determines the verb’s number, even when there’s another noun in between?

So if you have something like “The key to the cabinets is on the table,” the relevant noun is “key,” not “cabinets.” You can test whether the model prefers “is” to “are,” and then systematically vary what comes between the subject and the verb. That gives you a much more interpretable measure than overall language-model performance.

Looking back, I’d emphasize that this is a narrow diagnostic. Getting agreement right doesn’t establish that a model has acquired syntax in the full sense, and an error doesn’t tell you exactly what representation it lacks. But as a starting point, it was productive: it turned a broad debate about whether neural networks could learn syntax into specific questions we could investigate experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response describes agreement as a useful, interpretable diagnostic and cautions that it is narrow. It does not say researchers were initially surprised LSTMs could handle it or that, in retrospect, it was an easy test.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think it was a useful place to start because subject-verb agreement gives you a very simple way to ask whether a language model is sensitive to syntactic structure. You can compare something like “the key to the cabinets is” with “the key to the cabinets are.” To get that right reliably, the model needs to track the subject across an intervening noun that has a different number. Just agreeing with the most recent noun won’t work.

That made it a fairly clean diagnostic. We could vary the number of intervening nouns and look at where the model started making mistakes, rather than just asking whether its overall language-modeling performance was good.

But it’s also a narrow test. A model can succeed on many agreement examples using shortcuts, and success doesn’t establish that it has acquired human-like syntax in general. So I still think it was a good first probe. The important thing is to follow it with more controlled examples and a broader range of constructions, and to ask what mechanism is actually supporting the behavior.

r001.rationale: The response retrospectively calls subject-verb agreement a simple, useful diagnostic, but it does not mention researchers’ initial surprise or contrast that surprise with the later view that the test was easy for LSTMs.
